title: Ogre Holl and the Flow of Time
markdown:
The sun painted the highest Whispering peaks in pink and gold as if it had been commissioned. For Ogre Holl it was not an ordinary morning. He was very large and, more to the point, very earnest. Today he would meet Elder Gristle, whose words were said to sound like falling rock and whose ideas came clear as meltwater.

“Now then, Moss,” Holl boomed, a rumble that might have worried distant teacups. He smoothed his roughspun tunic and gave the napkin at his collar a decisive tug. “A splendid impression. I have rehearsed the opening address seventeen times.”

Moss, a ram of serious fleece and unshakeable loyalty, answered from beside Holl’s muddy boots with a bleat that suggested seventeen was a complete set and that a scratch behind the horns would be a better use of the hour.

Holl chuckled and obliged. Politeness, on him, sat oddly well. “A treat first, then.” He produced an apple of heroic size, polished to a boast, and presented it with a flourish the orchard had not requested.

They ambled. Orchards bowed under fruit until the branches seemed to greet them; the air mixed apple-sweet with mountain-crisp, a smell that made Holl want to add a line about ripening to the speech and then wisely not. Bees worked the late blossom as if they had not been told an Elder was expecting anyone. They passed watchtower ruins worn smooth by weather, stones that had forgotten the names of the people who stacked them. Holl pictured sentinels with granite hearts, which fitted the speech he was carrying, and practised the gesture that would accompany “yearning to bask” — a hand to the chest, napkin cooperating.

A drover with a string of bells nodded and did not ask for an address. A stream argued with a shelf of rock and won, as streams do. Holl named these things inwardly as scenery worthy of a preface. Moss named them as walking.

In a sun-dappled meadow he tried the opening at full theatrical boom: “Most esteemed Elder Gristle, I have journeyed from the green valley to bask in the bright glow of your deep wisdom, eager to learn all you know!” The echo came back flatter than he had budgeted for. He puffed his chest anyway.

Moss bleated, clearly, toward a patch of wild thyme beyond mossy boulders. Holl, who listened to his ram even when mid-sentence, steered them there and let the thyme happen. Juice and green scent. A rest that did not appear in the seventeen rehearsals and was, he admitted to the apple core, an improvement.

The path climbed after that, switchbacks that taught humility to napkins. Holl muttered comparisons about time — rivers, seasons, the way a shadow moves on a sundial if one has a sundial, which he did not. He did not notice, until much later, that he had an audience with feathers.

Twilight put violet on the ridges and a hush on the bees. They reached The Gilded Goblet, an inn of loud cheer and slightly argumentative walls, tucked in a gorge as if the mountain had agreed to a pocket of warmth. The sign’s charm outweighed its drawing: a cup that might have been gold if you stood far enough back and wanted it to be. Inside: roasted roots, cider opinions, boots drying by a hearth that believed in itself, a happy mess of travellers comparing passes. Fizzwick the goblin innkeeper moved through it with eyes like dark glass and a voice that cut cleanly, already pouring before the door had finished shutting.

“Well met! Holl the Hearty, and the fancy sheep. Stew bubbling. Cider of the year, I assure you.”

Holl beamed, confidence arriving with the heat. He ordered stew for himself, greens for Moss, and straightened the napkin as if thought required linen. “Fizzwick. I have been practising for Elder Gristle. A comparison, you see, about how time always moves forward.”

A harsh caw tore the rafters. A raven, glossy, bead-eyed, ruffled and fixed on Holl. The nearby tables went oddly still.

“Flow of time!” it croaked, a startling, mischievous copy of Holl’s own voice with a rasp added for style.

Holl’s cheeks went mortified crimson. He had, he now recalled, muttered on the path. Fizzwick raised one eyebrow. “An eloquent bird you have acquired.”

“He repeats. One phrase. An accident from earlier.”

The raven, sensing an audience, gave it again, dramatic: “Flow of time!”

Holl’s plans flattened. He tried the finest apples of the northern territories, said to grow in this very fold of hill. “Flow of time!” He praised the stew’s honesty, the cider’s year. “Flow of time!” He mentioned the weather, which was innocent. The raven was not. Nearby patrons began to smile into their mugs. One raised a cup to Holl as if he had booked the entertainment. Moss ate greens and declined to be drawn. Fizzwick, who had seen stranger houseguests, wiped a table and left the bird its stage.

Holl slept poorly in a room that listed a little toward the gorge, the phrase arriving whenever he found the edge of a dream. Moss snored with the peace of someone who had not compared time to anything.

Dawn came like gold poured over snow. A vast shadow filled the inn door. Elder Gristle stood in it, ancient and quiet with power, as if the threshold had been waiting for that exact silhouette.

Holl’s heart hammered. He stood, hunting the practised words. “Esteemed Elder Gristle, I have journeyed from the green valley to bask—”

“Flow of time!” shrieked the raven — Reginald, as the beam above Gristle’s head now implied — from a perch chosen for maximum timing.

Holl’s shoulders sagged. He could not, in conscience, continue. Fizzwick scurried with a chair and a dark steaming mug.

Gristle showed no annoyance. Amusement lived in the wrinkles. “Ah, Reginald. Still fond of big speeches.”

Holl blinked. “You know him?”

“Many seasons.” Gristle sipped. “He repeats what introduces a little chaos. He once kept me laughing two weeks about lost glasses.”

Understanding arrived on Holl’s face without needing a title. The Elder was not scoring the interruption. He was enjoying a colleague.

Gristle’s craggy smile widened. He did not explain wisdom. He nodded at Moss, who was chewing clover as if drama were a seasoning he could ignore, and at the raven, who looked pleased with his cue. “Sit,” he said. “The brew is better than the speech, and I have heard the speech.”

Holl sat. His voice, when it came, was ordinary size. “Thank you.”

Reginald offered one last, almost polite, “Flow of time!” and beat away into the bright, show concluded.

They ate. Steam from the mugs wrote small weather on the air. Greens disappeared in the methodical way Moss did everything. Fizzwick pretended not to listen and failed, because innkeepers are paid in other people’s pauses. Holl’s napkin stayed where it was; he did not tug it. Elder Gristle tore bread, spoke of a pass that had changed its mind after a slide, and did not ask for the rest of the address. The friendship, such as it began, started in the leftover quiet after a bird had stolen the opening. Holl kept that fact in his chest, unpolished, and asked for more stew. Outside, the peaks took the morning as if no one had rehearsed them. Time, for what it was worth, moved. The raven was already a speck, and then not even that.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
